hook: A student council of 8 seniors and 12 juniors says it chose 4 members "at random" to send to a conference. All 4 were seniors. The juniors cry foul. Could plain chance pick 4 seniors? You do not need a formula: imitate a random pick 100 times and see how often it happens.

prereq.q: Random digits are used to pick 4 of 20 students. A digit pair repeats one already chosen. What should you do?
prereq.why: When picking different people, skip repeats so each student is chosen once.

prereq.q: A dotplot of 100 values has 12 dots at 7 or more. What share of the values are 7 or more?

figure.caption: 100 simulated random picks of 4 members. Only 2 trials chose 4 seniors.

chain.cause: A chance process is hard to analyze with a formula
chain.effect: imitate it with a model that has the same chances (random numbers, a coin, a die)

chain.cause: Carry out the model once and record the result
chain.effect: one trial: here, the number of seniors among 4 random picks
the share of trials with the result estimates its probability (2 of 100 gave 4 seniors, about 0.02)
by the law of large numbers the estimate settles near the true probability

ideas: A simulation imitates a chance process with a model that has the same chances. Each repetition is a trial.
The probability of a result is the share of times it happens in a very long run of trials. A simulation estimates it with the share of its trials.
Describe a simulation so someone else could run it: the device and what each value means, what one trial is, what you record, how many trials.
The law of large numbers: as the number of trials grows, the share of trials with the result gets closer to the true probability.
A result that happens rarely in a simulation of a claim gives reason to doubt the claim.

misconception.wrong: A coin that has landed heads many times in a row is "due" for tails, so early streaks will be balanced out.
misconception.right: The coin has no memory. In the long run the share of heads approaches 0.5 because later flips swamp the early ones, not because tails catch up.

summary: To estimate a probability by simulation, model the chance process with a device that has the right chances, define one trial and what to record, repeat many trials, and use the share of trials with the result. More trials give a steadier estimate (the law of large numbers). A rare simulated result casts doubt on the claim behind the model.
